name: Equations of motion
subject: Physical Sciences
example_problem: A car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 25 m/s over 300 m. Choose the correct equation of motion, calculate the acceleration, and then the time taken.

importance.summary: Mechanics is the biggest Gr 12 Paper 1 section (65/150); momentum & impulse, vertical projectile motion and work-energy-power all build directly on these equations.

covered_by.topic: MECHANICS: Instantaneous speed and velocity and the equations of motion
covered_by.subtopic: Equations of motion in the horizontal plane; vehicle safety and stopping distance

diagnostic.prompt: A car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 25 m/s over 300 m. Its acceleration is:
options: 0,875 m/s² in the direction of motion

diagnostic.prompt: A problem gives vi, vf and Δx and asks for a. Which equation fits immediately?
options: vf² = vi² + 2aΔx - the one with no time in it

recap:
The equations of motion describe straight-line movement with UNIFORM (constant) acceleration - the word "uniformly" in a problem is your licence to use them at all. Five quantities star in every problem: initial velocity vi, final velocity vf, acceleration a, time Δt, and displacement Δx.

Four equations, each missing exactly one quantity: vf = vi + aΔt (no displacement); Δx = viΔt + ½aΔt² (no final velocity); vf² = vi² + 2aΔx (no time); Δx = (vi + vf)/2 × Δt (no acceleration - the average-velocity equation). That missing character is the whole secret of choosing. Every problem gives three quantities and wants a fourth; the fifth - neither given nor wanted - is absent, and the right equation is the one that EXCLUDES it. Never grab the first equation you remember: match the hole to the absent quantity.

Method: first list Given, Wanted and Absent formally, converting units as you list - km/h becomes m/s by dividing by 3,6 (90 km/h = 25 m/s), and skipping this poisons every later step. Then choose by the absent character, substitute with units, solve, and state vector answers with a direction.

Worked: a car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 25 m/s over 300 m. Given vi, vf, Δx; wanted a; absent: time - so vf² = vi² + 2aΔx. Substitute: 625 = 100 + 600a (write the squares out immediately - 25² is 625, not 25). Solve: a = 525/600 = 0,875 m/s² in the direction of motion. For the time: vf = vi + aΔt gives 15 = 0,875Δt, so Δt = 17,14 s.

Verify by a second road wherever possible: Δx = (vi + vf)/2 × Δt uses only ORIGINAL data - the average of 10 and 25 is 17,5, and 300 ÷ 17,5 = 17,14 s again. Two independent routes agreeing proves both answers; a wrong acceleration could not have hidden. Final habits: sense-check size and sign (a braking car has negative a in your chosen positive direction - keep vector signs consistent), and remember these same equations return in matric as vertical projectile motion with a = 9,8 m/s² downward.

exit_check.prompt: The equations of motion may only be used when:
90 km/h converted for use in the equations is:
Why is checking the time with Δx = (vi + vf)/2 × Δt such a strong verification?
options: It uses only original given data, so an error in the calculated acceleration cannot hide
It always gives a rounder number
